advances: The original third halfspace-depth moment has an absolute positive multiple of 8^{-n} on every decreasing log-affine positive-resource downset with at most an absolute constant times n rows. The proof retains the original denominator Z^4. A quartic auxiliary law supplies a coordinate surplus, one shared selection inflates only O(sqrt(nk)+k) rates, product association pays a linear resource cost, and one additional real score slab pays O(sqrt(n)). Every estimate for the new quartic law is proved here. This restricted theorem does not assert the locked mixed-integer conclusion.
author: research-agent
proof:
D contains zero and is finite, since the first positive row bounds every coordinate. Thus Z>0. If some R_r=0, its positive row forces D={0}, so M_3(p)=1 and the claimed inequality follows from 0<kappa<1. Assume from now on that all R_r>0.

First establish a generic bound for every present n and k. Use the count and reflected mass with exactly the meanings in accepted fact 4121ae9d64b2d14e:
\[
k_j=\#\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:j+v,j-v\in D\},\qquad
\mathsf H_j=k_jp_j
=\sum_{x\in D\cap(2j-D)}\sqrt{p_xp_{2j-x}}.
\]
The last equality follows from log-affinity, including zero displacement. For any centered closed halfspace H={x:u dot (x-j)>=0}, reflection about j sends every endpoint outside H into H. Pairing reflected endpoints, with boundary endpoints included in H, gives
\[
\mathsf H_j\le
2\sum_{x\in D\cap(2j-D)\cap H}\sqrt{p_xp_{2j-x}}
\le2\sqrt{\left(\sum_{x\in D\cap H}p_x\right)
\left(\sum_{x\in D\cap(2j-D)\cap H}p_{2j-x}\right)}
\le2\sqrt{p(H)}.
\]
The middle step is Cauchy--Schwarz; the second factor is at most one because reflection is injective. Taking the infimum proves tau_p(j)>=H_j^2/4. Also H_j<=1 by Cauchy--Schwarz on the full reflected sum.

Every ordered pair x,y in D of the same coordinatewise parity has an integer midpoint j=(x+y)/2 in D: nonnegativity and Az<=R are convex constraints. Conversely every term counted by k_j corresponds to precisely such a pair. Log-affinity gives p_x p_y=p_j^2. If P_c is the mass of parity class c in {0,1}^n, this bijection and Cauchy--Schwarz show
\[
\mathbb E_p\mathsf H_j=\sum_j k_jp_j^2
=\sum_{c\in\{0,1\}^n}P_c^2\ge2^{-n}.
\]
Consequently Jensen's inequality gives the exact generic bound
\[
M_3(p)\ge\frac1{64}\mathbb E_p\mathsf H_j^6
\ge\frac1{64}(\mathbb E_p\mathsf H_j)^6
\ge64^{-n}/64.
\tag{1}
\]
This proof needs no assumption that D is full dimensional.

Now define the new quartic generating function and law for s>0:
\[
F_4(q)=\sum_{u\ge0}(2u+1)^3q^u
=\frac{1+23q+23q^2+q^3}{(1-q)^4},\qquad
Q_s^{(4)}(u)=\frac{(2u+1)^3e^{-4su}}{F_4(e^{-4s})},\qquad
\mu_4(s)=\mathbb E_{Q_s^{(4)}}u.
\]
Here u is a coordinate index, not a resource index or a halfspace normal. The rational identity follows by expanding (2u+1)^3=8u^3+12u^2+6u+1 and differentiating the geometric series. This Q_s^{(4)} differs from the square coordinate law Q_{e^{-s}} in accepted facts 4121ae9d64b2d14e and 609407d6db81b18b.

We claim the uniform moment bounds
\[
\mathbb E_{Q_s^{(4)}}u^2\le13/s^2,\qquad
\mu_4(s)\le4/s\quad(s>0),\qquad
\mu_4(s)\ge1/(80s)\quad(0<s\le h).
\tag{2}
\]
To prove the first two, put q=e^{-4s} and P(q)=1+23q+23q^2+q^3. Let B take values 0,1,2,3 with respective probabilities 1,23q,23q^2,q^3 divided by P(q). Independently let N have probability binom(m+3,3)(1-q)^4 q^m at m>=0. Its generating function is ((1-q)/(1-qz))^4. Multiplying the generating functions of B and N shows that B+N has exactly law Q_s^{(4)}. Differentiating the displayed generating function yields
\[
\mathbb E N^2=\frac{4q+16q^2}{(1-q)^2}
\le\frac{20q}{(1-q)^2}
=\frac5{\sinh^2(2s)}\le\frac5{4s^2}.
\]
Also E B^2=(23q+92q^2+9q^3)/P(q)<=124e^{-4s}. The elementary maximum s^2e^{-4s}<=1/(4e^2) gives E B^2<=31/(e^2s^2)<5/s^2; for the strict numerical inequality, e>8/3 follows from the first four terms of its exponential series. Thus
\[
\mathbb E(B+N)^2\le2\mathbb E B^2+2\mathbb E N^2
\le\frac{25}{2s^2}\le\frac{13}{s^2}.
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz implies mu_4(s)<=sqrt(13)/s<=4/s.

For the lower bound, Q_s^{(4)} is the geometric law of ratio q, biased by the increasing function (2u+1)^3. The covariance of that function and u under the geometric law is nonnegative: it is half the expectation of the product of their differences at two independent copies. Dividing that covariance inequality by the expected bias gives mu_4(s)>=q/(1-q)=1/(e^{4s}-1). Convexity of e^{4s}-1 and its zero value at zero imply e^{4s}-1<=(s/h)(e^{4h}-1)=80s/h for s<=h. Since h=log3>1, the last bound in (2) follows. The inequality h>1 follows from e<3, itself given by 1/m!<=1/2^{m-1} for m>=2 with strict inequality for some m.

We also need the coordinate surplus
\[
(1-e^{-s})^4F_4(e^{-4s})\ge\alpha\quad(s>0).
\tag{3}
\]
Let P_s(u)=(1-e^{-s})e^{-su}, and put f_s(u)=(2u+1)P_s(u). With the alias rho=e^{-s}, the exact coordinate factor in accepted fact 609407d6db81b18b is
\[
\sum_uP_s(u)f_s(u)^2
=(1-e^{-s})^3\sum_u(2u+1)^2e^{-3su}\ge8/27.
\]
Holder's inequality gives (sum P_s f_s^2)^{3/2}<=sum P_s f_s^3. The latter sum is precisely the left side of (3), proving (3). All these sums converge because s>0. Moreover alpha>1/8: after squaring, this is 512/19683>1/64, equivalently 32768>19683. Hence delta_4>0.

For the new quartic dual construction set psi_4(s)=(1/4)log F_4(e^{-4s}) and phi_4(s)=max{0,psi_4(s)-psi_4(h)} for s>0, with phi_4(0)=+infinity. Differentiating the positive exponential series gives psi_4'(s)=-mu_4(s) and psi_4''(s)=4 Var_{Q_s^{(4)}}(u)>=0. Thus phi_4 is convex, vanishes for s>=h, and diverges at zero. In particular mu_4 is nonincreasing.

Minimize over lambda in R_{>=0}^k the function
\[
\mathcal F_4(\lambda)=\lambda\cdot R+
\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_4\left(\sum_{r=1}^k\lambda_ra_{ri}-\theta_i\right).
\tag{4}
\]
A sufficiently positive first multiplier gives a finite value. Because phi_4>=0 and every R_r>0, a finite sublevel is bounded. A minimizing subsequence has a limit in the closed orthant; divergence of phi_4 excludes any zero coordinate argument at that limit. Continuity at positive arguments proves attainment. Fix a minimizer and set
\[
t_i=\sum_r\lambda_ra_{ri},\qquad s_i=t_i-\theta_i>0,
\qquad\mu_i=\mu_4(s_i),\qquad\Lambda=\lambda\cdot R.
\tag{5}
\]
The meanings of t_i,s_i,Lambda are the shifted dual scores, rates, and capacity pairing in accepted fact 4121ae9d64b2d14e, now for the optimizer of (4). No identity with its optimizer is assumed. Since theta_i<=0, 0<=t_i<=s_i and |theta_i|<=s_i. A zero multiplier vector is allowed; then positivity of s_i forces every theta_i<0. If any theta_i=0, the multiplier vector cannot be zero. No law at a zero rate occurs.

There is x satisfying
\[
x_i=\mu_i\ (s_i<h),\quad x_i=0\ (s_i>h),\quad
0\le x_i\le\mu_i\ (s_i=h),\qquad
Ax\le R,\quad\lambda_r(R_r-a_r\cdot x)=0\ (1\le r\le k).
\tag{6}
\]
Here is the full argument for ties and inactive multipliers. Let X_0 be the displayed tie box with its untied coordinates fixed, let G_0={R-Ax:x in X_0}, and let Q_0 be the closed cone whose r-th coordinate is zero when lambda_r>0 and nonnegative when lambda_r=0. If G_0 and Q_0 were disjoint, their positive distance would be attained, since G_0 is compact and Q_0 closed. For a nearest pair g_0,u_0 put v=u_0-g_0. Minimizing distance along segments yields v dot g<=v dot g_0 for g in G_0 and v dot u>=v dot u_0 for u in Q_0. Taking u=0 and u=2u_0 gives v dot u_0=0, so max_{g in G_0}v dot g<=-||v||^2<0. Also v_r>=0 whenever lambda_r=0, by testing the corresponding positive coordinate rays in Q_0. Thus v is a feasible direction at lambda.

The directional derivative of (4) in direction v is exactly max_{x in X_0}v dot (R-Ax). At a tied coordinate the derivative is max{0,-mu_i sum_r v_ra_{ri}}, which is maximization over its interval 0<=x_i<=mu_i; at an untied coordinate it is the ordinary derivative. All present s_i are positive, so the derivative is within its domain. The strictly negative derivative contradicts minimality. Therefore G_0 meets Q_0, proving (6), including lambda=0.

Choose an extreme point of the compact nonempty polytope in (6). At most k tied coordinates are strictly between 0 and mu_i, since otherwise a nonzero vector supported on more than k such coordinates and annihilated by all k rows permits small perturbations in both directions preserving all constraints. Define I_0={i:x_i=mu_i} and I_*={i:0<x_i<mu_i}. From (2), (5), (6) and this choice,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|I_*|&\le k,&\Lambda&=\sum_i t_ix_i,&
\sum_{i\in I_0}a_{ri}\mu_i&\le R_r,\\
s_i&\le h\quad(i\in I_0),&s_i&\ge h\quad(i\notin I_0),&
\sum_{i\in I_*}t_ix_i&\le4k.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
The equality uses complementary slackness with t, not s.

Apply accepted fact 9ec030107c9689ad with its parameter equal to K, its dimension and row count n,k, and entries w_{ri}=a_{ri}mu_i on I_0 and zero elsewhere. Delete selected zero columns outside I_0. This yields I subset I_0 such that, with U_r=sum_{i in I}a_{ri}mu_i,
\[
|I|\le K\sqrt{nk}+k,\qquad
\sum_{i\in I_0\setminus I}(a_{ri}\mu_i)^2\le U_r^2/K^2.
\tag{8}
\]
If I_0 is empty, choose I empty directly. If I_0 is nonempty, positivity of each row on I_0 and (8) force I nonempty, and every U_r>0. No row normalization is required.

Define s_i'=Ks_i for i in I and s_i'=s_i for i in I_0 minus I. Let Q be the product law with coordinate J_i of law Q_{s_i'}^{(4)} on I_0 and J_i=0 deterministically off I_0. Write nu_i=E_Q J_i on I_0. Monotonicity and (2) give
\[
\nu_i\le\mu_i\quad(i\in I_0),\qquad
\nu_i\le\frac4{Ks_i}\le\frac{320}{K}\mu_i\le\mu_i/4\quad(i\in I),\qquad
\mathbb E_Q J_i^2\le13/(s_i')^2\quad(i\in I_0).
\tag{9}
\]
For any real row b define sigma_b(j)^2=sum_i b_i^2j_i(j_i+1)/3. In particular sigma_r means sigma_{a_r}, and sigma_theta uses the original theta row. If I_0 is nonempty, (7)--(9) imply
\[
\mathbb E_Q(a_r\cdot J)\le R_r-3U_r/4.
\tag{10}
\]
Each of Var_Q(a_r dot J) and E_Q sigma_r(J)^2 is at most
\[
83200\sum_{i\in I_0}\frac{(a_{ri}\mu_i)^2}{(s_i'/s_i)^2}
\le166400U_r^2/K^2\le U_r^2/48^2.
\tag{11}
\]
Indeed 1/s_i<=80mu_i on I_0, so (9) bounds each variance term by 13 times 80^2=83200 times the displayed squared weight. For the displacement variance use J_i(J_i+1)<=2J_i^2 on nonnegative integers, whose coefficient is at most the same 83200. The selected squared weights sum to at most U_r^2/K^2, and the unselected squared weights do so by (8). Finally 166400 times 48^2=383385600<K^2=1073741824.

Let G_r={a_r dot J+sigma_r(J)<=R_r}. Chebyshev and Markov give, with joint probability at least 7/8,
\[
a_r\cdot J\le\mathbb E_Q(a_r\cdot J)+4\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_Q(a_r\cdot J)},
\qquad\sigma_r(J)\le4\sqrt{\mathbb E_Q\sigma_r(J)^2}.
\]
Each exceptional probability is at most 1/16. Zero variance or zero squared expectation makes the corresponding condition automatic. By (10)--(11), the total increase is at most 8U_r/48=U_r/6, smaller than the margin 3U_r/4. Thus Q(G_r)>=7/8. If I_0 is empty, J=0 and every G_r holds identically.

For the original score width, (5), (9), and J_i(J_i+1)<=2J_i^2 give
\[
\mathbb E_Q\sigma_\theta(J)^2
\le\frac{26}{3}\sum_{i\in I_0}\frac{\theta_i^2}{(s_i')^2}
\le9n.
\]
Hence the event B_theta={sigma_theta(J)<=12sqrt(n)} has Q-probability at least 15/16. It holds identically when sigma_theta is zero.

Every G_r and B_theta is coordinatewise decreasing, since all resource entries are positive and j_i(j_i+1) increases on nonnegative integers. Independent coordinates positively associate these events, exactly as proved in accepted fact 4121ae9d64b2d14e. To check applicability directly, decreasing bounded functions f,g of one variable have covariance equal to half E[(f(X)-f(X'))(g(X)-g(X'))]>=0. The conditional covariance identity and induction over independent coordinates give the same property for a product law; conditioning leaves both conditional means decreasing. Applying this to decreasing intersections gives, for G=B_theta intersect intersection_r G_r,
\[
Q(G)\ge(15/16)(7/8)^k,
\qquad D_G:=-\log Q(G)\le d_0k+d_1,
\qquad G\subseteq D.
\tag{12}
\]
The last inclusion refers to integer roots in the support of Q.

Put T=t dot J and M_Q=E_Q T. Equations (7)--(9) show that
\[
0\le\Lambda-M_Q
=\sum_{i\in I_*}t_ix_i+\sum_{i\in I}t_i(\mu_i-\nu_i)
\le4k+4|I|.
\tag{13}
\]
Every other term vanishes. For u>=0 define ell(u)=log E_Q exp[-u(T-M_Q)]. Exponential tilting changes each nondeterministic coordinate to the same quartic law at rate s_i'+ut_i/4. Thus (2) and 0<=t_i<=s_i<=s_i' imply
\[
\ell''(u)=\sum_{i\in I_0}t_i^2
\operatorname{Var}_{Q_{s_i'+ut_i/4}^{(4)}}(J_i)
\le\sum_{i\in I_0}\frac{13t_i^2}{(s_i'+ut_i/4)^2}\le13n.
\]
The rates are positive and all derivatives exist; t_i=0 leaves its law unchanged. Since ell(0)=ell'(0)=0, ell(u)<=13nu^2/2. Restrict its defining expectation to G and apply conditional Jensen to obtain ell(u)>=-D_G+u(M_Q-E_Q[T|G]). Consequently, for u>0,
\[
M_Q-\mathbb E_Q[T\mid G]\le D_G/u+13nu/2.
\]
Optimizing when D_G>0, and taking u down to zero when D_G=0, combines with (13) to give
\[
\mathbb E_Q[T\mid G]\ge
\Lambda-4k-4|I|-\sqrt{26nD_G}.
\tag{14}
\]
If lambda=0 then t=0, Lambda=0 and T=0, so all these inequalities apply without a positive multiplier assumption.

For j in G take V_i independently uniform on the integers {-j_i,...,j_i}. Apply accepted fact 4d7d60d01a9ce8e5 with its n present coordinates and k+1 arbitrary real rows equal to a_1,...,a_k,theta. Its variances are exactly the sigma_b(j)^2 just defined. The event E_j where every |a_r dot V|<=sigma_r(j) and |theta dot V|<=sigma_theta(j) therefore satisfies
\[
\#E_j\ge e^{-C_{\mathrm{slab}}(k+1)}\prod_i(2j_i+1).
\tag{15}
\]
This includes every zero-variance row. For each allowed V, both j+V and j-V are nonnegative integer vectors and satisfy every resource inequality because j in G. They lie in the original D. Moreover
\[
p_{j+V}=p_je^{\theta\cdot V}\ge p_je^{-12\sqrt n},
\qquad p_{j-V}\ge p_je^{-12\sqrt n}.
\]
The set E_j is invariant under V to -V and contains zero. For every original closed halfspace through j, at least half its endpoint vectors j+V lie in that halfspace, including boundary endpoints. Distinct V give distinct endpoints. Thus (15) proves the original-law bound
\[
\tau_p(j)\ge\frac12p_j e^{-12\sqrt n-C_{\mathrm{slab}}(k+1)}
\prod_i(2j_i+1)\quad(j\in G).
\tag{16}
\]
No auxiliary tilted law is used to measure this halfspace mass.

Since the multipliers are nonnegative, t dot z<=Lambda for every z in D. With theta_i=t_i-s_i, the original denominator satisfies
\[
Z\le e^\Lambda\prod_i(1-e^{-s_i})^{-1}.
\tag{17}
\]
Let Z_Q=product_{i in I_0} F_4(e^{-4s_i'}), with empty products equal to one. On the support of Q, all other coordinates are zero, and its exact normalization yields
\[
\prod_i(2j_i+1)^3e^{4\theta\cdot j}
=Z_Q Q(J=j)\exp\left(4\sum_{i\in I_0}(s_i'+\theta_i)j_i\right)
\ge Z_Q Q(J=j)e^{4t\cdot j}.
\tag{18}
\]
The inequality uses s_i'+theta_i>=s_i+theta_i=t_i and j_i>=0. Cubing (16), multiplying by the original p_j, summing over G, and using (17)--(18) and conditional Jensen gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_3(p)
&\ge\frac18e^{-36\sqrt n-3C_{\mathrm{slab}}(k+1)}
Z_Q\prod_i(1-e^{-s_i})^4
Q(G)e^{4(\mathbb E_Q[T\mid G]-\Lambda)}\\
&\ge\frac18\exp\left[-36\sqrt n-3C_{\mathrm{slab}}(k+1)
-D_G-16k-16|I|-4\sqrt{26nD_G}\right]
Z_Q\prod_i(1-e^{-s_i})^4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]
The normalization before (17) is exactly the original Z^4, since p_j tau_p(j)^3 supplies p_j^4=e^{4theta dot j}/Z^4. The event G is contained in the finite set D, so its conditional positive exponential expectation is finite even if an unrestricted such expectation would diverge.

For i in I_0 minus I, its coordinate factor in the last product of (19) is at least alpha by (3). For i off I_0, (7) gives (1-e^{-s_i})^4>=(1-e^{-h})^4=16/81>alpha. The last comparison follows by squaring: 256/6561>512/19683. It includes every dropped fractional tie coordinate. Finally, for i in I,
\[
\frac{F_4(e^{-4Ks_i})}{F_4(e^{-4s_i})}\ge\frac1{48K^4}.
\tag{20}
\]
Indeed the numerator polynomial 1+23q+23q^2+q^3 is between 1 and 48 for 0<=q<=1. The positive integer K satisfies 1-e^{-Kv}<=K(1-e^{-v}) by the geometric-sum identity. Combining these facts at v=4s_i proves (20). Therefore (3) and (20) bound the product in (19) below by alpha^n(48K^4)^{-|I|}. Equations (12) and (19) become
\[
M_3(p)\ge\alpha^n
\exp\left[-b_4|I|-(3C_{\mathrm{slab}}+d_0+16)k
-36\sqrt n-3C_{\mathrm{slab}}-d_1-\log8
-4\sqrt{26n(d_0k+d_1)}\right].
\tag{21}
\]
This includes I_0 empty, when Q is concentrated at zero and all its product factors are empty.

If k<=n, (8), k<=sqrt(nk), and sqrt(d_0k+d_1)<=sqrt(d_0k)+sqrt(d_1) bound the entire price in (21) by M_4 sqrt(nk)+L_4 sqrt(n)+C_4. Hence
\[
M_3(p)\ge\alpha^n
\exp[-M_4\sqrt{nk}-L_4\sqrt n-C_4]\quad(1\le k\le n).
\tag{22}
\]
Now assume k<=epsilon n. This ensures k<=n and M_4 sqrt(nk)<=delta_4 n/4. For n>=N_4, the definitions of N_4 also give L_4 sqrt(n)<=delta_4 n/4 and C_4<=delta_4 n/4. Since alpha=e^{delta_4}/8, (22) gives M_3(p)>=e^{delta_4 n/4}8^{-n}>=8^{-n}>=kappa 8^{-n}.

For n<N_4, the exact generic bound (1) gives M_3(p)>=8^{-n}(8^{-n}/64)>=8^{-n}(8^{-N_4}/64)=kappa 8^{-n}. Together with the zero-capacity case, this proves the theorem for every stated instance, including all ties, inactive multipliers, zero score coordinates, and real positive row entries.
statement:
Let n,k>=1 be integers, A=(a_{ri}) in R_{>0}^{k x n}, R in R_{>=0}^k, and theta in R_{<=0}^n. Write a_r for row r and define
\[
D=\{z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n:Az\le R\},\qquad
Z=\sum_{z\in D}e^{\theta\cdot z},\qquad
p_j=e^{\theta\cdot j}/Z\quad(j\in D).
\]
The original closed-halfspace depth and its third moment are
\[
\tau_p(j)=\inf_{u\in\mathbb R^n}
\sum_{z\in D:\,u\cdot(z-j)\ge0}p_z,
\qquad M_3(p)=\sum_{j\in D}p_j\tau_p(j)^3.
\]
Including u=0 does not change the infimum. Moving the boundary of any closed halfspace containing j to j can only decrease its mass, so this is exactly the infimum over all original closed halfspaces containing j.

Use the following explicit absolute constants, with natural logarithms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=32768,& h&=\log3,& \alpha&=(8/27)^{3/2},& \delta_4&=\log(8\alpha)>0,\\
C_{\mathrm{slab}}&=\frac{2\log64}{1-\sqrt{7/8}},&
d_0&=\log(8/7),&d_1&=\log(16/15),\\
b_4&=16+\log(48K^4),\\
M_4&=(K+1)b_4+3C_{\mathrm{slab}}+d_0+16+4\sqrt{26d_0},\\
L_4&=36+4\sqrt{26d_1},&C_4&=3C_{\mathrm{slab}}+d_1+\log8,\\
\epsilon&=\min\{1,(\delta_4/(4M_4))^2\},\\
N_4&=\left\lceil\max\{1,(4L_4/\delta_4)^2,4C_4/\delta_4\}\right\rceil,&
\kappa&=8^{-N_4}/64.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then, whenever 1<=k<=epsilon n, one has M_3(p)>=kappa 8^{-n}. The assertion includes arbitrary real positive rows, zero capacities, tied rates, inactive multipliers, a zero multiplier vector, theta coordinates equal to zero, and deterministic auxiliary coordinates.

The constant C_slab is exactly the constant in accepted fact 4d7d60d01a9ce8e5. The shared-selection parameter of accepted fact 9ec030107c9689ad is the present K, not the moment prefactor kappa. The coordinate factor from accepted fact 609407d6db81b18b is used with its geometric ratio rho=e^{-s}. We use the product-association argument and shifted-rate meanings of accepted fact 4121ae9d64b2d14e, but construct a new quartic optimizer and prove all its moment estimates below; its square-law optimizer and auxiliary law are not reused.
